extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators and undergraduate mathematics majors (mathematics instructors, researchers in math education)
extracted.subtask_short: proof reading strategies for math proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for how students should read and comprehend mathematical proofs (strategies students can use to improve proof comprehension). Focuses on undergraduate/proof-oriented courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrase theorem in own words (Strategy 1a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should restate the theorem in their own words to ensure they understand the assumptions and conclusions and to make the claim an object of thought before reading the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps students understand the meaning of claims and the proof framework to be used. In the survey (Study 2) a majority of mathematicians preferred this strategy (≈67.4% preferred students do this; 18.1% neutral; 14.5% preferred they not). Use rephrasing to clarify what is being assumed and what must be shown; this supports anticipating proof structure rather than getting lost in line-by-line detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the theorem in first-order logic (Strategy 1b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing the theorem formally in first-order logic as a way to clarify its logical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This more formal implementation of Strategy 1 was seldom endorsed by surveyed mathematicians (majority ≈66.3% preferred students not do this; only ≈19.3% preferred it). The paper notes it was used by participants in only one case (Theorem 4) and may be beneficial in narrow contexts, but is generally not recommended as a routine strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to prove the theorem before reading its proof (Strategy 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to prove the theorem yourself (even briefly) prior to reading the provided proof to motivate reading and to anticipate the proof framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides motivation and helps students predict the approach and structure the proof will use. The survey found very strong preference for this strategy among mathematicians (≈88.0% preferred students attempt this). Caveat: trying to prove first is not merely verification; it should be used to anticipate framework and increase engagement rather than to only check correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider proof frameworks (attend to assumptions, conclusions, and technique) (Strategy 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the high-level framework or structure of the proof (e.g., what propositions are being proved, how subclaims relate, what technique—contradiction, induction, bounding—will be used) before or while reading details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps students see why assumptions and conclusions are appropriate and how the proof is organized. The paper emphasizes naming subclaims (e.g., P and Q) to facilitate understanding and social interaction. Survey results show a majority prefer this strategy (≈63.9% preferred), but a notable minority preferred an alternative phrasing (≈22.9% preferred the foil), indicating some disagreement about how to prioritize frameworks vs other starting points. Use this strategy to avoid becoming mired in low-level algebraic manipulations before seeing the proof's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break the proof into parts / sub-proofs (Strategy 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition long or complex proofs into lemmas, sub-proofs, or manageable chunks and, if useful, delay detailed reading of sub-lemmas to focus on the high-level argument first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partitioning makes complicated proofs manageable and facilitates summarization. Example from transcripts: students skipped the lemma's detailed proof initially to focus on how the lemma is used, then returned to the lemma for technical details. Survey shows strong support (≈88.0% preferred students use this). Guidance: explicitly locate where subproofs/lemmas begin and end; if structure is not clearly signaled in the text, students should annotate and mark boundaries themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate assertions with specific examples (Strategy 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a step or inference is confusing, instantiate the statement with a concrete example (e.g., n = 24) to see why the inference holds and to clarify the role of terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples can be used both to empirically verify a statement and to illuminate why a general claim holds. The paper distinguishes two uses: using an example to verify versus using it as a generic instance to reveal the mechanism (the latter helps understanding more deeply). Survey support was substantial (≈71.1% preferred). Practical advice: choose an example that reflects the structure of the claim; avoid mistaking mere verification for a proof of the general statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare the proof method with one’s own methods (Strategy 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the technique used in the proof with how you would have approached the problem to identify novel or useful methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes the method itself an explicit object of discussion, helps learners acquire new techniques, and aids transfer to future problems. Transcript evidence shows this fosters appreciation of novel techniques; survey support was high (≈86.7% preferred). Use this strategy to catalog useful ideas and to reflect on when alternative approaches might be advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical caveats and implementation notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations and cautions about teaching or prescribing these strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The qualitative study had a small sample and a limited set of proofs; the paper does not claim exhaustive coverage of all useful strategies (e.g., drawing diagrams, tracking where hypotheses are used may also be useful). The authors note that identifying strategies is a first step and that effective instruction to teach them requires careful design (address content knowledge, beliefs, and prescriptive implementation). Thus, while mathematicians largely desire students to use these strategies, instructors should consider instructional scaffolding and practice opportunities rather than merely listing strategies.
